slides: So, we've learned how to write the heart of the essay. The argument paragraphs, and the rebuttal paragraph.
Now we wrap it. And we start with the paragraph that opens the essay... the opening paragraph.
So what is the opening paragraph for? Well, it has two jobs. One for the essay, and one for the rater.
For the essay, it sets the scene. We're about to discuss an issue, so the opening gives the background to the dispute,
then it presents the dispute itself, and then, off we go, the discussion can start.
Now, for the rater, it has a different job. This is where you make your first impression.
The rater picks up your essay, starts reading, and this is the first time they meet your writing.
Let me take you into a rater's head for a moment.
As they read, paragraph by paragraph, they get closer and closer to the scores they want to give you. Content, and language.
Officially, a rater should only give the score at the end. After reading everything, and going through the rubric.
But, I mean, after hundreds and thousands of essays, it just happens on its own. There's already a score in their head.
So they finish your opening and they think: okay, language five, let's keep going.
And with every paragraph after that, they ask themselves: am I still at five? Oh, this impressed me, now it's six. Or... hmm, this went down to four.
So what can the rater learn from your opening? Language, clearly. They see the language you use, and they set a starting level.
And content? Well, that's hard to judge from an opening paragraph. Why?
Because almost everyone's opening is very similar. The background, the dispute. Everyone writes more or less the same thing,
often in almost the same sentences, because they all take it from the task text.
So where are essays different? In the body. Different arguments, different explanations, different examples, comparisons and weakenings.
So for the rater, the opening sets your starting language level. If you can give its language a little extra attention, do it.
Now, what goes into the opening paragraph? Three parts.
One: background. What came before the dispute, why there's a dispute now, where it all started.
Two: the dispute. We describe the question we're discussing.
Sometimes we also add what each side thinks, with or without a main argument. You don't have to. Some people add one side, some add both, some add neither.
And if you do add an argument, just give the claim itself. Only the key sentence. Don't start explaining it or developing it here. That comes later, in the argument paragraphs.
And three: at the end of the paragraph, we write our own position.
Okay, a small note about the position.
You don't have to write it at the end of the opening. You could put it at the start of the next paragraph, somewhere in the middle, even in the closing.
But what we recommend is... write it at the end of the opening paragraph.

Because a lot of students who don't do this end up with an essay where the main thread jumps from one side to the other. The essay stops holding together, and the rater thinks: wait, are you for or against?
And you lose nothing by saying it early. You don't need to keep the rater in suspense, and you don't need to surprise anyone in the closing.
Just tell them your position, as clearly as you can, and carry on from there.
Remember, the content of the opening is the same for everyone. It's a template. So don't be creative here. Write what's needed, and move on.
And everything you need for it is already in the task text. The background, the sides, the dispute, even arguments, if you want to add them.
Think about it. The task text is almost a perfect opening. It gives the background, it describes the dispute.
There's only one difference. Instead of a personal position at the end, it asks you: what's your opinion? And that's exactly where your opening ends... with your position.
So what we recommend is to rewrite the relevant parts in your own words.
But you can also copy parts. Is there a phrase or a sentence that's worded really well? Take it.
Copying segments of the task text is fine. A phrase that's worded well, a key term, one sentence.
But don't copy the whole task word for word. Choose the parts you need, make them shorter, and connect them with your own words.
Because the opening should show that you understood the issue. And a copied block of text... doesn't show that.
So what does this mean for you? Don't get stuck. You can rewrite it? Great. You can't? Take the key segments, link them in a sentence or two of your own, and move on to the essay.

And like we said in the bridging recommendation lesson, a complex position can go here, instead of a bridging recommendation in the rebuttal paragraph. It's a good option, if you can keep its boundary clear and logical.
Now, try to avoid sentences that don't move you forward.
Okay. How does that help? It doesn't. It adds nothing to the content, and it hurts the focus.
Every sentence should add something. Background, the dispute, or your position. Nothing else.
And don't try to impress, or be creative, in the opening.
Why? Because the content is the same for everyone. I mean, how much creativity can you really show in an opening? So just let it go.
Rewrite the task text in the simplest, most standard way you can, and keep moving. Want to impress? Do it in the body.
One small exception, though. If there's something in your language you can lift a little, the opening is a good place for it. It's the first impression.
For example, instead of 'many people are against it', you write 'this proposal has met with considerable opposition'. Precise, formal, but not flowery.
Do you know that famous drawing of a horse? Try to guess which side the artist started from.
Well, the artist started from the back. A perfect tail, almost like a photo. Lots and lots of time went into it.
And then slowly... wait, the time, the deadline. Okay, let's colour a little less. Let's hurry.
And the part that always kills me is the front leg. It's just one thin line. Let it go, and run.
That's what happens when the deadline gets close. And you have thirty-five minutes for the whole essay.
So you don't want a perfect, polished opening, maybe even creative, and then the rest of the essay falls apart.
So maybe the most important thing about the opening is this: don't waste time on it. Take the background, describe the dispute in short, state your position, and run to the essay. Impress there.
